analysis.title: "Rekt": McElligott Says The Bond Short-Squeeze Just Blew Up Every "High Sharpe" Trend Trade
key_insights: Nomura's Charlie McElligott says the defining market feature is a sweeping loss of cross-asset momentum that accelerated last week. His note is titled DE-TRENDED. He traces it to a squeeze in bond shorts, where lower yields are triggering reversals in anti-dollar FX and in small cap and value equities (anything non-AI).

Nomura's cross-asset momentum factor is down 4.01% over five days and 2.72% month-to-date. US equities momentum is the worst at -5.87% on the week and -7.08% MTD, against a +7.29% YTD gain. Interest-rate swap trend strategies are losing in both the US and Europe.

Inside equities McElligott calls it reverse dispersion, with everything else outperforming the legacy AI winners. Equal-weight vs the S&P is up a 2.2-sigma move over five days, short-term reversal is +1.8 sigma, and the high-minus-low momentum factor is down 2.5 sigma (6.8%) on the week.

McElligott does not see a full macro regime change yet. He frames it as crowded high-Sharpe trend trades reversing, where profit-taking turned into a broader risk-management de-grossing, mostly among leveraged funds and starting in the bond short.

Nomura's QIS trend model flags almost every major bond contract as Reversing. USD 30Y futures returned 3.25% last week and USD 20Y 2.77% (1.87 z-score on a five-year lookback). All of those contracts still show negative trailing Sharpe ratios on every horizon from three months to five years.

The same reversal flags show up across G10 FX and short-term rate futures, including EURUSD, GBPUSD, SOFR and Euribor. The Bloomberg dollar index fell 0.4% to its lowest since September 30 on Iran compromise-proposal headlines.

The bond and STIR reversals started as profit-taking in crowded shorts around hot inflation prints, then grew into a covering squeeze. A hot print is a reasonable time to monetize a short instead of risking a violent squeeze on a weak data day. The 10Y ended a week of hotter-than-expected CPI at a three-week low.

CTAs were caught wrong-way. Nomura's CTA replication portfolio lost 2.0% last week (9th percentile) and the SG Trend index fell 1.7%. The past month is negative but the year is +12.7% YTD. Since October 1, bonds account for roughly 1.5 points of the CTA drawdown, with small additional losses from equities, STIRs and G10 FX.

Legacy AI positioning was liquidated on negative catalysts: the Anthropic ARR trajectory, CoreWeave and neocloud sustainability, and credit and financing costs. South Korean data-center firm Elice fell more than 30% in its trading debut.

Nomura's AI Enablers vs Hyperscalers pair fell 11% last week and 12% over the past month, with a past-week Sharpe of -22.7 and a 25.7% peak-to-trough drawdown this year. It is still up 34% YTD. The Semi-Energy Barbell slipped to +61% YTD from +65% on Oct 9.

The de-grossing lifted unwanted stocks. Legacy shorts and underweights in defensives and cyclical value outperformed popular longs. This matches Goldman Prime data showing hedge funds sold every dollar of AI stock bought since January 2025.

McElligott sees the latest Iran headlines as a positive surprise that could catalyze the underweighted Left Behind stocks and push the energy shortage, inflation and hawkish central bank worst case lower again. This matches his Oct 9 BINARIES note, where a conciliatory Iran deal into the midterms would hit energy and rate vol and favor gold and IWM upside. Tehran denied that a deal is close as the note circulated and oil bounced off its lows.

McElligott does not think last week marked capitulation into a growth scare or recession base case. He says it could still arrive quickly if higher rates, wider credit spreads and sticky energy prices sharply tighten financial conditions and cause demand destruction.

Client flows are in low-strike receivers and curve caps, which pay off in a growth scare or an Iran-deal relief rally. Nomura's swaptions desk says the left-hand side of the vol surface (1y1y, 1m10y) has likely flipped to receivers over in aggregate, while the intermediate-to-long end stays skewed payers over.

OCC data through Friday show one-week net call demand at the 100th percentile for ETFs and 98th for single stocks (five-year lookback), with put demand at the 5th and 19th percentiles. McElligott reads it as buy-side stock replacement: cutting underlying exposure while buying cheap upside to avoid missing a year-end rally.

ZeroHedge's own view is more skeptical than McElligott's. It cites the Iran denial, record-low pending home sales, housing starts at 1.221 million, and AI financing stress in credit, and bets the growth scare arrives before an Iran deal. Earnings from META and TSLA are due Wednesday.

tension_points.bull_case: McElligott says this is a mechanical unwind of crowded high-Sharpe trend trades, not a macro regime change, and that a pre-midterm Iran deal could unleash the Left Behind stocks.
tension_points.bear_case: ZeroHedge says the Iran deal was denied within hours, growth data keeps rolling over (record-low pending home sales, weak housing starts), credit is pricing AI financing stress, and swaptions and client flows show hedging toward lower rates.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Higher rates, wider credit spreads and sticky energy prices sharply tightening financial conditions into demand destruction would turn the crowding unwind into a growth scare.

tension_points.bull_case: A conciliatory Iran deal before the midterms would hit energy and rate vol and favor gold and IWM upside, repricing the energy shortage and hawkish central bank worst case lower.
tension_points.bear_case: Tehran denied that a deal is close, and oil bounced off its lows.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Tehran's denial that Iran-US talks continue and that reports a deal is close.
